job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based only on the supplied text, these are the principal loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems. Some may be policy choices rather than unintended defects; whether they would control in practice could depend on regulations, other law, and interpretation.

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—single-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-metric-ton threshold applies “by a single vessel,” with no rule aggregating vessels, operators, or related activity. An operation could argue that recovery divided among multiple vessels falls below the definition’s threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—undefined measurement period and scope.** “Per year” does not say whether the measure is a calendar year, a rolling period, or a projected rate, and the text does not specify how to count mixed or processed material. That leaves uncertainty about when the threshold is crossed and what recovery counts.

3. **Section 2(1)(B)—open-ended discretion.** The Secretary may classify other activities as commercial mining based on comparable ecosystem risks, but the bill supplies no criteria, process, or deadline for that determination. Until a determination is made, an operator could argue its activity is outside the definition; the provision also invites disputes over the Secretary’s authority and reasoning.

4. **Section 2(1)—unclear reach beyond the defined activity.** The definition covers recovery of nodules or “other mineral resources,” but does not say how it applies to prospecting, collection of samples, processing, or related support work. Those activities may be argued to fall outside “recovery” or “engage in” commercial mining.

5. **Section 2(2)—narrow definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition covers citizens and corporations organized under State law, but not expressly other entities or individuals such as partnerships, LLCs, permanent residents, or trusts. It also does not address a foreign entity’s U.S. subsidiaries or affiliates, leaving uncertainty about who is covered when activity is conducted through them.

6. **Section 2(3)—narrow vessel definition.** Registration applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons equipped for mineral recovery. Smaller vessels and vessels not equipped for recovery are outside that definition, even though Section 3’s prohibition is not limited to covered vessels.

7. **Sections 2(1), 3(a)—undefined “engage in.”** The bill does not specify whether “engage in” includes financing, contracting, transporting, processing, or providing services to a mining operation. That uncertainty could support arguments that particular participants or support activities are outside the prohibition.

8. **Section 3(a)—uncertain territorial scope.** “Any person in the United States” could refer to a person’s presence in the country or to conduct there; the text does not define the relevant U.S. territory or specify how the clause applies to offshore conduct. The separate U.S.-person clause reaches only the persons defined in Section 2(2), creating potential coverage gaps.

9. **Section 3(b)—broad existing-license exception.** The exception has no express end date or limits on the scale, location, or type of mining it protects. It also does not specify who must have issued the exploration license or whether that license must authorize the mining conducted, leaving room for disputes over which pre-enactment licenses qualify.

10. **Section 3(c)—unbounded environmental-assessment exception.** The exception has no definition of “environmental assessment,” limits on the amount or duration of recovery, or requirement for independent approval. An operator could argue that otherwise prohibited recovery is exempt if conducted for assessment purposes.

11. **Sections 3, 4—different activity and vessel coverage.** The prohibition applies to commercial mining by any covered person, while registration and reporting apply only to operators of covered vessels. The bill therefore creates no corresponding tracking or reporting requirement for potentially prohibited activity using smaller vessels or other methods.

12. **Section 4(a)—no registration deadline or procedure.** The bill does not say when a vessel must register, what information the registration must contain, or what happens if it does not. That makes the requirement difficult to administer and enforce as written.

13. **Section 4(b)—incomplete reporting requirements.** “Quarterly” is not tied to a filing deadline, reporting format, or specific required data beyond a description of recovery activities. The text also does not establish consequences for late, incomplete, or inaccurate reports.

14. **Section 5(a)—penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Civil penalties are stated to apply to violations occurring on or after enactment, but Section 8 delays the Act’s effective date by 180 days. The text does not clarify whether conduct during that interval can be penalized, or how that language interacts with the delayed prohibition.

15. **Section 5—enforcement mechanics are missing.** The bill does not identify the agency or process for assessing civil penalties, address notice or review, or specify how penalties are calculated for continuing conduct. The criminal provision likewise does not identify a specific fine amount, instead referring generally to fines under Title 18.

16. **Section 6—international-agreement duty is vague.** “Seek to negotiate” does not require an agreement to be reached, and the text does not specify what counts as seeking negotiations or what happens if no agreement is reached within 18 months. “Equivalent” prohibitions are also undefined.

17. **Section 7(a)—unclear termination mechanism.** The bill does not specify how the National Academies report is initiated, what it must contain, or whether Congress must act by a particular date. The requirement that Congress find mining can occur “without serious harm” supplies no standard for applying that phrase.

18. **Section 7(b)—sunset may override the duration provision.** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect until a joint-resolution finding, but Section 7(b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect after 10 years. The bill does not say whether the prohibition can continue beyond that date if Congress has not made the finding.

19. **Section 8—effective date does not distinguish provisions.** The 180-day delay applies to the whole Act, without stating whether it delays registration, reporting, or the international-negotiation deadline as well as the prohibition. That creates uncertainty about when each obligation begins.
